text: Some time later David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up to one of the cities of Judah?" The LORD said to him, "Go up." David asked, "Where shall I go?" He answered, "To Hebron."
So David went up there, along with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel.

versions.text: So David went up there, along with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads simply "wife of Nabal" (אֵשֶׁת נָבָל), the standard designation used for her elsewhere. "Widow" is an interpretive addition; keeping "wife" stays closer to the text without losing sense, since Nabal's death is already known.

text: David also brought up the men who were with him, each with his household, and they settled in the towns around Hebron.
Then the men of Judah came and there anointed David king over the house of Judah. When David was told that it was the men of Jabesh-gilead who had buried Saul,
he sent messengers to them with this word: "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this kindness to your lord, to Saul, and buried him.
Now may the LORD show you steadfast love and faithfulness, and I too will do good to you because you have done this.
Now then, let your hands be strong, and be valiant men, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."

versions.text: So take courage now and be strong, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."
versions.explanation: The current rendering flattens two distinct Hebrew clauses ("let your hands be strong" and "be sons of valor") into a near-redundant pair ("take courage... be strong"). Restoring the two images preserves the idiom and reads well aloud.

text: Meanwhile Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul's army, had taken Ish-bosheth son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim,
and made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin—over all Israel.
Ish-bosheth son of Saul was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David.
The length of time David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner set out from Mahanaim to Gibeon with the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul.
Joab son of Zeruiah and David's servants also set out, and they met them at the pool of Gibeon. One company sat down on one side of the pool, the other on the opposite side.
Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men get up and fight before us." Joab said, "Let them get up."
So they got up and were counted off: twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of David's servants.

Each man seized his opponent by the head and drove his sword into his side, and they fell together. That is why the place at Gibeon is called Helkath-hazzurim.^[The name means "field of sword edges," or "field of flints."]

versions.text: Each man seized his opponent by the head and drove his sword into his side, and they fell together. That is why the place at Gibeon is called Helkath-hazzurim, the Field of Sword Edges.
versions.explanation: The inline gloss interrupts the narrative rhythm at the close of the verse; the Hebrew gives only the name. Moving the explanation to a footnote keeps the oral flow while retaining the information.

versions.text: That is why the place at Gibeon is called Helkath-hazzurim.^[The name means "field of sword edges," or "field of flints."]
versions.explanation: The first half of the verse has been lost. The Hebrew states that each man grasped his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent's side, and that they fell together — this is the whole point of the naming that follows. The earlier revision only moved the name's gloss into a footnote; it did not intend to delete the combat description. Restored from the prior wording, with the footnote retained.

text: The fighting that day was fierce beyond measure, and Abner and the men of Israel were beaten by David's servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel was as fleet of foot as a wild gazelle.
Asahel chased after Abner, swerving neither right nor left as he pursued him.
Abner looked back and said, "Is that you, Asahel?" "It is," he answered.
Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right or your left; take on one of the young men and strip him of his gear." But Asahel would not stop chasing him.
Again Abner said to Asahel, "Stop chasing me! Why should I strike you to the ground? How could I ever look your brother Joab in the face?"

But he refused to turn aside, so Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, and the spear came out through his back. He fell there and died on the spot. And everyone who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died stopped there.
But Joab and Abishai kept up the pursuit of Abner. As the sun was going down, they came to the hill of Ammah, which lies opposite Giah on the road to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjaminites rallied behind Abner, formed a single band, and took their stand on the top of a hill.
Then Abner called out to Joab, "Must the sword devour forever? Don't you know that this will end in bitterness? How long before you order your men to stop pursuing their brothers?"
Joab answered, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, the men would not have given up the pursuit of their brothers until morning."
So Joab blew the ram's horn, and all the troops halted; they no longer pursued Israel or continued the fight.
Abner and his men marched through the Arabah all that night. They crossed the Jordan, went on through the whole Bithron, and came to Mahanaim.
When Joab turned back from pursuing Abner, he gathered all the troops. Nineteen of David's servants were missing, besides Asahel.
But David's servants had struck down three hundred and sixty men of Benjamin, from among Abner's forces; all of them died.

versions.text: But David's servants had struck down three hundred sixty of Benjamin and of Abner's men, and they were dead.
versions.explanation: "and they were dead" is redundant and awkward after "struck down." The revised wording keeps the Hebrew's final verb ("died") while reading more naturally aloud.

text: They carried Asahel away and buried him in his father's tomb at Bethlehem. Then Joab and his men marched all night, and daybreak found them at Hebron.
